scenes.title: “It works on my machine”
scenes.narration: It works on my machine. Docker is how you stop saying that.

steps.say: Your app runs here, but on the next computer something it needs is missing.
Docker packs your app and everything it needs into one box.
And that box runs the same on any computer.
It was first shown at PyCon, in March 2013.

scenes.narration: So it's a virtual machine? No.

steps.say: A virtual machine runs a whole operating system, kernel and all.
A container is one walled off process that shares the host's kernel.
So many more of them fit on one machine.

scenes.narration: You describe the box in a Dockerfile.

steps.say: Start from a small image that has Node.
Install your packages, then copy in your code.
Say what to run, then build it.
steps.output:
$ docker build -t my-app .
 => [1/5] FROM docker.io/library/node:22-alpine
 => [2/5] WORKDIR /app
 => [3/5] COPY package*.json ./
 => [4/5] RUN npm install
 => [5/5] COPY . .
 => naming to docker.io/library/[my-app]{good}

scenes.narration: That build makes an image: read only layers, one for each step.

steps.say: Each one is stacked on the base.
Change your code, and only the top layer is built again.
The rest come from the cache.

scenes.title: An image becomes a container
scenes.narration: Run the image, and you get a container.

steps.say: It starts in the background, port eighty eighty reaches the app inside, and it answers.
The Dockerfile is the recipe, one layer per step.
The image is what it builds: a read only template.
A container is that image, running, the same on every machine.
